title: Musculoskeletal Connective Tissue: Origins, Collagen, Cartilage, and Elastic Fibers
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains where the connective tissues of bone, cartilage, tendon, and ligament come from, which collagen types build them, how collagen and elastic fibers are assembled, and why cartilage and tendon heal slowly. Board questions usually name a vitamin, mineral, gene, or embryonic tissue and ask which structure or step fails. If you can place each defect on the collagen pathway, explain how charged proteoglycans hold water, and describe how fibrillin-1 controls TGF-beta, you can reason through most questions on scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta, Menkes disease, osteoarthritis, and Marfan syndrome.
prerequisites: Germ layers, somites, and neural crest formation (MS-1)
Histology of bone, cartilage, and dense connective tissue (MS-2)
Protein synthesis in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi apparatus, and secretion
Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked inheritance
Structure of the vertebral column and synovial joints (MS-3, MS-4)

connections.how: Vitamin C, iron, and copper are cofactors for collagen modification, so dietary deficiency becomes a connective tissue disease.
COL1A1, COL1A2, ATP7A, and FBN1 mutations show how the type of mutation (null allele or dominant negative) sets disease severity.
Osteoarthritis begins with proteoglycan loss and collagen network damage in avascular articular cartilage that cannot repair itself.
Fibrillin-1 and type III collagen defects weaken the arterial wall, causing aortic root dilation, dissection, and arterial rupture.
Type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane is the target in Alport syndrome and Goodpasture syndrome.

terms.def: Loosely organized embryonic connective tissue whose cells migrate and differentiate into fibroblasts, chondroblasts, and osteoblasts.
The ventromedial part of each somite that surrounds the notochord and neural tube and forms the vertebrae and ribs.
Cells that leave the edges of the neural folds, migrate widely, and in the head form most of the facial skeleton and connective tissue.
The secreted triple helical precursor of collagen that still carries its nonhelical propeptides at both ends.
The collagen molecule left after the propeptides are cleaved, which self-assembles into fibrils.
A copper-dependent extracellular enzyme that converts lysine side chains to aldehydes, which then form covalent cross-links in collagen and elastin.
A long unbranched polysaccharide of repeating disaccharides, usually sulfated and strongly negatively charged.
The large cartilage proteoglycan whose core protein carries many chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains and binds hyaluronan.
Cartilage in which dense type I collagen bundles alternate with rows of chondrocytes, resisting both tension and compression.
A large glycoprotein that forms the microfibrils on which elastin is deposited and that anchors latent TGF-beta in the matrix.
A cross-link formed from four lysine side chains that joins elastin molecules and lets the fiber recoil after stretch.
A mutation whose abnormal product interferes with the normal product from the other allele, producing a worse phenotype than loss of one allele.

sections.title: Embryonic origins of bone, cartilage, and tendon

blocks.text: Every skeletal connective tissue begins as mesenchyme, which condenses where a bone, cartilage, or tendon will form. Three sources supply this mesenchyme in different body regions: the somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm in the limbs, the sclerotome of the somites in the axial skeleton, and neural crest in most of the face. Because the sources are separate, a defect in one can damage a single region while the rest of the skeleton is normal.

blocks.title: Sources of musculoskeletal connective tissue
rows: Limb bones and cartilage, limb tendons and ligaments, limb dermis and fascia, sternum
Vertebrae, ribs, annulus fibrosus, occipital part of the skull base
Skeletal muscle fibers of the trunk and limbs (not their tendons in the limb)
Nucleus pulposus of each intervertebral disc
Most facial bones, pharyngeal arch cartilages, parts of the cranial vault, facial dermis and tendons
Mostly intramembranous (face and vault); arch cartilages are endochondral or persist as cartilage
blocks.caption: Each region of the skeleton has its own mesenchymal source, which is why regional malformations occur.

blocks.text: Limbs: skeleton and muscle meet after migration

The limb bud is a core of somatic lateral plate mesoderm under a cap of ectoderm. This core condenses into hyaline cartilage models that later ossify, and it also forms the tendons, ligaments, and connective tissue sheaths that pattern each muscle. The muscle cells themselves do not arise here. Myoblasts migrate into the bud from the somites, so a limb muscle and its tendon come from different sources and join only after migration, guided by the lateral plate connective tissue.
Axial skeleton: the sclerotome and resegmentation

Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and neural tube floor plate induces the ventromedial somite to become sclerotome. Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome fused with the cranial half of the next, a process called resegmentation, shown below. The shift places each segmental muscle across an intervertebral joint so it can move the spine, and lets the spinal nerve exit near the disc. Failure of segmentation fuses vertebrae (in the neck, Klippel-Feil syndrome, with a short neck, low hairline, and limited motion), and failure of one half to form gives a hemivertebra and congenital scoliosis.

blocks.title: From somite to vertebra
steps: Notochord and floor plate secrete Sonic hedgehog
Ventromedial somite becomes sclerotome
Sclerotome cells surround the notochord and neural tube
Each sclerotome splits into cranial and caudal halves
Caudal half fuses with the next cranial half
Fused halves form the vertebral body; intervening cells form annulus fibrosus
Notochord persists between bodies as nucleus pulposus
blocks.caption: Resegmentation makes vertebrae intersegmental, so muscles from one somite span two vertebrae.

blocks.text: Head: neural crest builds the face

Cranial neural crest cells migrate into the frontonasal region and the pharyngeal arches. There they form most of the viscerocranium (maxilla, mandible, zygomatic, nasal, and palatine bones) by intramembranous ossification, and the cartilages of the first two arches, including Meckel cartilage, the malleus, incus, and stapes. Paraxial mesoderm supplies the occipital region and much of the posterior skull base. When neural crest cells are too few, as in Treacher Collins syndrome, the mandible, zygomatic bones, and ears are hypoplastic while the limbs and spine are normal, which the origins in the table predict.

blocks.predict: An infant has fused cervical vertebrae, a normal face, and normal limbs. Which embryonic tissue failed, and why are the face and limbs spared?
blocks.explain: The sclerotome failed to segment. The face comes from neural crest and the limb skeleton from somatic lateral plate mesoderm, so neither depends on sclerotome segmentation.
blocks.check: The source table and the resegmentation flow.

sections.title: Collagen types and the tissues they build

blocks.text: Collagens are a family of proteins built from three alpha chains wound into a triple helix. The fibrillar collagens (types I, II, III, and V) lose their end domains after secretion and pack into banded fibrils, while type IV keeps its nonhelical domains and forms a network. Each tissue uses the type whose architecture fits the load it carries, so knowing the load predicts the collagen.

blocks.title: Collagen types to know
rows: Thick fibrils in parallel bundles; two alpha1(I) chains and one alpha2(I) chain
Bone, tendon, ligament, dermis, fibrocartilage (annulus fibrosus, menisci, pubic symphysis), dentin, cornea, mature scar
Highest tensile strength; about 90% of body collagen
Thin fibrils dispersed in proteoglycan gel; three alpha1(II) chains
Hyaline and elastic cartilage, nucleus pulposus, vitreous body
Restrains proteoglycan swelling so cartilage resists compression
Fine fibrils forming branched reticular fibers
Reticular stroma of lymph nodes, spleen, marrow, and liver; blood vessels; uterus; skin; early granulation tissue
Flexible support in distensible organs and early repair
Basement membranes, including the external lamina of each muscle fiber and the glomerular basement membrane
Supports epithelium and muscle fibers and filters
Fibrillar, regulates type I fibril diameter
With type I in skin, tendon, and other tissues
Hypertrophic chondrocytes of the growth plate
blocks.caption: Types I to IV are the core exam set; types V and X are added because they appear in musculoskeletal disease.

blocks.text: Type I collagen dominates tissues pulled in tension. In tendon and ligament its fibrils lie parallel to the line of pull, and in bone it forms the organic scaffold (osteoid) on which hydroxyapatite deposits, giving bone tensile strength while the mineral resists compression. Fibrocartilage is a hybrid: dense type I bundles resist tension, and a small amount of proteoglycan around rows of chondrocytes resists compression. In the intervertebral disc the outer annulus fibrosus is mainly type I, while the gel-like nucleus pulposus is type II with abundant proteoglycan.

Type II fibrils are thin and do not bundle, and their refractive index is close to that of the surrounding matrix, so hyaline cartilage looks glassy and fiber-free on light microscopy. Its matrix stains basophilic because of the sulfated GAGs, not the collagen. Type III fibrils are heavily glycosylated, which is why reticular fibers are periodic acid-Schiff positive and stain black with silver (argyrophilic) rather than with H&E. In wound healing, type III is laid down first in granulation tissue and is gradually replaced by type I, which explains why a scar gains strength over months.

Type IV collagen keeps interruptions in its Gly-X-Y sequence and its terminal NC1 domains, so molecules link end to end and side to side into a mesh that binds laminin. In the glomerulus, alpha3, alpha4, and alpha5 chains form this mesh: Alport syndrome (most often X-linked COL4A5) causes hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects, and Goodpasture syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against the NC1 domain of the alpha3 chain.

sections.title: Collagen synthesis and the diseases of each step

blocks.text: Fibroblasts, osteoblasts, and chondrocytes modify and fold collagen inside the cell, then trim and cross-link it outside. Each step has its own requirement, so each defect can be placed on the pathway.

blocks.title: Collagen synthesis
steps: RER ribosomes make pro-alpha chains with Gly-X-Y repeats
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases act (vitamin C, Fe2+, O2)
Some hydroxylysines are glycosylated
C-propeptide disulfides align three chains; helix zips toward N-terminus
Procollagen passes through the Golgi and is secreted
Procollagen peptidases cleave both propeptides, forming tropocollagen
Tropocollagen self-assembles into staggered fibrils
Lysyl oxidase (copper) forms covalent cross-links
blocks.caption: Steps 1 to 5 occur inside the cell and steps 6 to 8 outside it.

blocks.text: Glycine occupies every third position because only its hydrogen side chain fits in the crowded center of the helix. Proline in the X and Y positions stiffens each chain, and hydroxyproline adds hydrogen bonding that keeps the helix stable at body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F). The hydroxylases are iron enzymes that use O2 and alpha-ketoglutarate, and ascorbate keeps their iron in the reduced Fe2+ state. Hydroxylysine provides sites for glycosylation and for the most stable cross-links.

Folding starts at the C-terminal propeptides, which also keep procollagen soluble inside the cell. Once they are cleaved outside, tropocollagen molecules pack in a quarter stagger, leaving regular gaps that give the fibril its banding and seed bone mineral. Lysyl oxidase then oxidizes lysine and hydroxylysine side chains to aldehydes that bond covalently with neighboring molecules, converting a weak fibril into one that resists tension.

blocks.title: Defects by step
rows: Fractures with minor trauma, blue sclerae (thin sclera shows the choroid), hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta
Unstable helices are degraded: perifollicular hemorrhage, bleeding gums, poor wound healing, subperiosteal hemorrhage
Loss of N-propeptide cleavage (ADAMTS2, or COL1A1 or COL1A2 cleavage site)
Disordered fibrils: fragile skin or joint dislocation
Weak collagen and elastin: tortuous arteries, bladder diverticula, lax skin
blocks.caption: The step that fails predicts which tissues fail.

blocks.text: Scurvy shows first where collagen turns over quickly and supports small vessels, so skin and gum capillaries bleed and wounds stay weak. Osteogenesis imperfecta is usually autosomal dominant: a null allele halves normal collagen and gives the mild form, while a glycine substitution gives severe or lethal forms, as the example below shows. Menkes disease is X-linked; ATP7A normally pumps copper out of enterocytes and into the Golgi for copper enzymes, so copper is trapped in the gut, serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low, and lysyl oxidase, tyrosinase (hypopigmentation), and cytochrome c oxidase (hypotonia, seizures, neurodegeneration) all fail; the brittle, kinky hair reflects poor copper-dependent cross-linking.

blocks.title: Why a glycine substitution in COL1A1 is worse than a null allele
blocks.text: Type I collagen has two alpha1 chains and one alpha2 chain. With one null COL1A1 allele, the cell makes about half the normal amount of collagen, but every molecule is normal: mild osteogenesis imperfecta. With a glycine substitution, half the alpha1 chains are abnormal and both kinds are used. A molecule is normal only if both of its alpha1 chains are normal, a probability of 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. About three quarters of the molecules carry at least one defective chain and are degraded or weaken the fibril. This is the dominant negative effect.

blocks.predict: A patient with scurvy and a child with Menkes disease both have fragile vessels. Where on the pathway does each defect lie, and which one also affects hair and the brain?
blocks.explain: Scurvy blocks hydroxylation inside the cell; Menkes blocks cross-linking outside it because lysyl oxidase lacks copper. Only Menkes also starves tyrosinase and cytochrome c oxidase.

sections.title: How articular cartilage resists compression, and why cartilage and tendon heal slowly

blocks.text: Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage about 70% to 80% water by weight, with sparse chondrocytes in lacunae, a type II collagen network, and a large amount of aggrecan. It has no blood vessels, nerves, or lymphatics, and unlike most hyaline cartilage it has no perichondrium. Its job is to spread load and give a nearly frictionless surface, and both depend on how its matrix handles water.

Aggrecan is a core protein carrying many chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains. Many aggrecan molecules (often 100 or more) bind noncovalently to a single strand of hyaluronan, stabilized by link protein, forming enormous aggregates trapped in the collagen mesh. The sulfate and carboxyl groups give the matrix a high density of fixed negative charge. These charges draw in Na+ and other cations, and water follows by osmosis, so the matrix tries to swell. The type II collagen network resists that swelling and is held in tension, much as the fabric of a tire holds in air pressure. The result is a pre-stressed cushion that pushes back when compressed.

blocks.title: Load and recovery in articular cartilage
steps: Joint load compresses the matrix
Fluid pressure rises and carries most of the load
Water escapes slowly through tiny matrix pores
Fixed charges concentrate; osmotic resistance rises
Load is removed
Fixed charges draw water and solutes back in
blocks.caption: Low permeability lets fluid pressure bear load, and cyclic loading pumps nutrients from synovial fluid to chondrocytes.

blocks.text: Because cartilage is avascular, chondrocytes receive nutrients and oxygen by diffusion from synovial fluid, aided by this pumping, and they work at low oxygen tension. They are few, cannot migrate through the dense matrix, and divide little in adults. Injury therefore brings no clot, no inflammatory cells, and no new matrix-forming cells. In osteoarthritis, proteoglycan loss lowers the fixed charge density, so cartilage loses stiffness, the collagen network fibrillates, and the damage spreads rather than heals.

Tendons are dense regular connective tissue: parallel type I collagen bundles with rows of flattened tenocytes. Cells are sparse and the blood supply is poor, reaching the tendon from the muscle, the bone insertion, and the surrounding paratenon or synovial sheath, with relatively avascular zones in the supraspinatus tendon near its insertion and in the Achilles tendon a few centimeters above the calcaneus. Healing passes through inflammation, a proliferative phase rich in type III collagen, and remodeling toward type I over many months, and the repaired tendon rarely regains full strength.

blocks.title: Blood supply and repair
rows: Little or none; defects reaching bone fill with fibrocartilage
Peripheral tears can heal; inner tears usually do not
Slow scar formation, type III then type I; strength stays below normal
Regenerates true bone without a scar
blocks.caption: Repair capacity tracks blood supply and the number of cells able to make new matrix.

blocks.title: Two cartilage injuries
blocks.text: A shallow defect in the articular cartilage of the femoral condyle never reaches bone. No vessels are injured, no clot forms, and nearby chondrocytes cannot migrate into it, so it persists or enlarges. A deeper defect that penetrates the subchondral bone bleeds. The clot brings marrow mesenchymal cells, which fill the defect with fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen. This tissue resists tension but lacks the aggrecan-rich, type II matrix that resists compression, so it wears down under joint loading. Vascular access, not the size of the injury, decides whether any repair occurs.

Elastic fibers let tissues stretch and spring back. Each fiber has an amorphous core of elastin, about 90% of the fiber, deposited on a scaffold of fibrillin-1 microfibrils about 10 nm wide. Cells secrete tropoelastin, a soluble precursor rich in glycine, proline, valine, and alanine with lysine-containing cross-linking domains. It contains little hydroxyproline, no hydroxylysine, and is not glycosylated. The microfibrils come first and guide tropoelastin into place, and lysyl oxidase, the same copper enzyme that cross-links collagen, joins four lysine side chains into desmosine and isodesmosine cross-links.

Elastin's hydrophobic segments are disordered. Stretching straightens them and lowers their entropy; releasing the force lets them return to disorder, so recoil is passive and needs no energy. The cross-links keep the molecules joined so the fiber returns to its original length. Elastic fibers stain poorly with H&E and are shown with special stains such as Verhoeff or orcein.

blocks.title: Collagen fibers versus elastic fibers
rows: Ligamentum flavum, elastic cartilage of the ear and epiglottis
blocks.caption: Both fibers depend on copper, which is why Menkes disease weakens arteries and skin.

blocks.text: The ligamenta flava join the laminae of adjacent vertebrae and form part of the posterior wall of the vertebral canal. Their high elastic content keeps them taut in every position. They stretch during flexion and recoil to help restore the upright posture, and their tension prevents them from buckling into the canal during extension. With age, elastic fibers are lost and the ligament thickens and folds inward, which contributes to lumbar spinal stenosis.

Fibrillin-1 microfibrils also store growth factor. TGF-beta is secreted in an inactive large latent complex: the mature cytokine bound to its latency-associated peptide, which is linked to latent TGF-beta binding protein. That binding protein attaches to fibrillin-1, holding TGF-beta in the matrix until integrins or proteases release it. In Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant FBN1 mutation on chromosome 15 leaves the microfibrils defective and unable to hold the complex, so TGF-beta is released and signals excessively through SMAD proteins. The mechanical weakness and the excess signaling together explain the phenotype: ectopia lentis (the lens zonules are microfibrils, and the lens usually shifts upward), mitral valve prolapse, aortic root dilation with cystic medial degeneration, tall stature with long limbs and arachnodactyly, and joint hypermobility. Loeys-Dietz syndrome, caused by TGF-beta receptor mutations, produces similar aortic disease, which supports the role of TGF-beta signaling.

blocks.title: Marfan syndrome pathogenesis
steps: FBN1 mutation produces defective fibrillin-1
Microfibrils are weak and reduced
Latent TGF-beta is not held in the matrix
Excess TGF-beta signaling disrupts smooth muscle and matrix
Elastic lamellae of the aortic media fragment
Aortic root dilates; dissection risk rises
blocks.caption: Structural weakness of the microfibrils and excess TGF-beta signaling act together on the aortic wall.

blocks.predict: Why does a fibrillin-1 defect dislocate the lens, while an elastin gene deletion (as in Williams syndrome) narrows the aorta above the valve but leaves the lens in place?
blocks.explain: Lens zonules are made of fibrillin microfibrils without elastin, so only fibrillin defects weaken them. Elastin loss affects elastic arteries, where too little elastin leads to smooth muscle overgrowth and supravalvular aortic stenosis.
blocks.check: The elastic fiber structure and the Marfan paragraph.

integration.text: Embryology, histology, and biochemistry explain the same tissues from three directions. The embryonic source decides where a malformation appears, the collagen type decides what load a tissue can carry, and the synthetic step decides which nutrient or gene matters. Vitamin C and iron act inside the cell and copper outside it, so scurvy and Menkes disease both weaken vessels but only Menkes, which starves many copper enzymes, damages the brain and hair. Elastic fibers and collagen share lysyl oxidase but differ in scaffold, which is why fibrillin defects dislocate the lens and elastin defects do not.

Pathology follows blood supply and cell number. Avascular articular cartilage and poorly perfused tendon cannot mount a full repair, so degenerative disease and tendon injury tend to persist, while well-vascularized bone regenerates. Immunology joins in at the basement membrane, where autoantibodies to type IV collagen cause Goodpasture syndrome. The limits of these rules matter: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has many types with different genes, Marfan features overlap with other connective tissue disorders, and TGF-beta excess is one contributor to aortic disease rather than the whole explanation.

summary: Limb bones, cartilage, and tendons come from somatic lateral plate mesoderm, limb muscle from somites, the axial skeleton from sclerotome, and most of the face from neural crest.
Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next; the notochord persists as the nucleus pulposus.
Type I collagen resists tension in bone, tendon, ligament, and fibrocartilage; type II restrains proteoglycan swelling in hyaline cartilage and the nucleus pulposus.
Type III forms reticular fibers and early granulation tissue; type IV forms the basement membrane network targeted in Alport and Goodpasture syndromes.
Glycine at every third position allows the triple helix; hydroxylation needs vitamin C and Fe2+; cross-linking by lysyl oxidase needs copper.
Scurvy fails at hydroxylation, osteogenesis imperfecta at type I chain structure or amount, and Menkes disease at copper-dependent cross-linking.
A glycine substitution acts dominant negatively, leaving only about one quarter of type I molecules normal, so it is worse than a null allele.
Aggrecan's fixed negative charges draw in cations and water, and the type II network holds that swelling, so cartilage resists compression.
Avascular cartilage and poorly perfused tendon heal slowly or poorly; cartilage defects reaching bone fill with weaker fibrocartilage.
Elastic fibers are elastin cross-linked by desmosine on fibrillin-1 microfibrils; FBN1 mutation in Marfan syndrome releases TGF-beta and weakens the aorta and lens zonules.

verify: The exact contribution of somites versus lateral plate mesoderm to the scapula and pectoral girdle, and of neural crest versus paraxial mesoderm to individual cranial vault bones, differs between sources; the chapter states only the consensus pattern.

Langman assigns the laryngeal cartilages to the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches, while some newer sources derive them from lateral plate mesoderm; the chapter does not name a source for them. Confirm which NABNE expects.
Water content of articular cartilage (about 70% to 80%) and the number of aggrecan molecules per hyaluronan strand (quoted from about 100 to 200) vary between sources and are given as approximate.
The share of elastin in an elastic fiber (about 90%) and microfibril diameter (about 10 nm, sometimes 10 to 12 nm) are approximate.

Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the Sillence classification of osteogenesis imperfecta and the current named types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (classical, vascular, kyphoscoliotic, arthrochalasia, dermatosparaxis), or only the main forms.
The location of the Achilles tendon hypovascular zone is quoted in different ranges (often about 2 to 6 cm above the insertion); the chapter says only a few centimeters.
